title: The Small Model Infrastructure Nobody Built (So We Did) — Filip Makraduli, Superlinked

primary.label: Inference & Model Systems
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 99%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is serving small models in production through an inference engine with batching, routing, autoscaling, and hot-swapping. The system is open-source infrastructure for builders and is specifically used in AI search and document processing with vector databases. The talk covers building the inference engine, deploying it with Terraform and Helm, and operating it in production with monitoring. Requires familiarity with inference concepts, GPU provisioning, attention mechanisms, and infrastructure tooling. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct excerpts from the talk.

summary: Filip Makraduli opens by acknowledging that despite his AI research and engineering background, inference—specifically how models run in production with GPU scheduling, routing, and automation—was a blind spot. He joined Superlinked to build an open-source inference engine called Sie (SIE) for small models focused on AI search and document processing, tested with vector DBs like Chroma, Qdrant, Weaviate, and LanceDB. The talk is structured around three key points. First, why this matters: context rot (quality degrading as context increases) necessitates small models for preprocessing and tool calling in agentic workflows. Community examples include Karpathy's graph-based knowledge bases and Chroma's context-filtering model. Superlinked used their engine for taxonomy classification in e-commerce via tool calling. Second, misconceptions: adding more GPUs is wasteful for small models that occupy only a few gigabytes; instead, hot-swapping multiple models on one GPU with LRU eviction improves utilization and lowers costs. Also, inference is not just the server—productionizing requires routing, autoscaling, queuing, and Prometheus/Grafana monitoring, which no open-source solution currently provides end-to-end. Third, the yin and yang of inference: model support (yin) requires supporting hundreds of diverse architectures—BERT, Qwen, ColBERT, rerankers, cross-encoders—each with different flash attention implementations, positional embeddings, normalization, and QKV fusion constraints. They re-implement forward passes to handle variable-length flash attention and token-based batching without wasted padding. Infrastructure (yang) includes a router, queuing mechanism, spot instances, and larger GPUs, with KEDA auto-scaling driven by Prometheus metrics to switch models dynamically and avoid idle GPUs. The key design goal is providing cluster and model support together as an end-to-end solution where models are simply configuration that can be swapped via Terraform apply. Both the inference engine and cluster are open-sourced with Helm charts and Docker images. The talk concludes with an audience Q&A about sinusoidal positional encodings used in transformer training.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Small model inference infrastructure is a market gap: no open-source solution previously provided end-to-end productionizing with routing, autoscaling, monitoring, and model support together.
Context rot—quality degradation as context increases—makes small models valuable for preprocessing and tool calling in agentic workflows before invoking larger models.
Provisioning one GPU per small model wastes idle memory; hot-swapping multiple models on a single GPU with LRU eviction dramatically improves utilization and lowers costs.

Supporting diverse model architectures (BERT, Qwen, ColBERT, cross-encoders) requires re-implementing forward passes to handle differences in flash attention, positional embeddings, normalization, and QKV fusion.
Sie's infrastructure uses KEDA auto-scaling with Prometheus metrics to dynamically switch models, avoid idle GPUs, and distribute workloads across spot instances and larger GPUs.
Models are treated as configuration that can be swapped via Terraform apply, with published Helm charts and Docker images for deployment.
Both the model inference component and the cluster infrastructure have been open-sourced, enabling end-to-end use without separate hardware provisioning or custom glue code.
Variable-length flash attention avoids wasting compute on padded tokens during token-based batching when requests have different token counts.
Understand why small model inference infrastructure matters for agentic workflows and context management
Recognize misconceptions about inference being solely about adding GPUs or server-side code

sections.title: Introduction and motivation
sections.summary: Filip introduces himself, references a Substack article on flash attention and memory vs. compute-bound processes where he overlooked inference as a key aspect. He joined Superlinked to build an open-source inference engine for small models in AI search and document processing.

sections.title: Why inference matters for agentic workflows
sections.summary: Explains context rot from Chroma research—quality degrades as context increases. Small models for preprocessing and tool calling help manage context. Cites Karpathy's knowledge graphs, Chroma's filtering model, and Superlinked's e-commerce taxonomy classification use case.

sections.title: What inference is not
sections.summary: Dispels misconceptions: more GPUs isn't the answer for small models occupying only a few gigabytes; hot-swapping on one GPU with LRU eviction improves utilization. Inference is also not just the server—productionizing needs routing, autoscaling, queuing, and monitoring, which no open-source solution currently provides end-to-end.

sections.title: Yin: Model support challenges
sections.summary: Discusses the need to support hundreds of open-source models with different architectures—BERT, Qwen, ColBERT, rerankers—each with different flash attention, positional embeddings, normalization, and QKV fusion. They re-implement forward passes for variable-length flash attention and efficient token-based batching.

sections.title: Yang: Infrastructure overview
sections.summary: Introduces the infrastructure layer with three API primitives: encode, score, and extract. A detailed infrastructure diagram is referenced for the deep dive.

sections.title: Infrastructure deep dive and open-source launch of Sie
sections.summary: Details the infrastructure: a router and queuing mechanism for load distribution across spot instances and larger GPUs, with KEDA auto-scaling driven by Prometheus metrics to dynamically switch models and avoid idle GPUs. The design goal is providing cluster and model support together as an end-to-end solution where models are configuration swapped via Terraform apply, with published Helm charts and Docker images. Both the inference engine and cluster are open-sourced under the name Sie (SIE). Concludes with an audience Q&A identifying sinusoidal positional encodings in transformer training.
